reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: An extremely common, benign disorder of follicular keratinisation producing rough, gritty, keratotic follicular papules with a goose-flesh texture
Classically affects the extensor upper arms, thighs, buttocks, and cheeks in a symmetrical distribution
Often accompanied by perifollicular erythema; a variant with prominent redness and atrophy affects the face (keratosis pilaris rubra and atrophicans)
Strongly associated with atopic dermatitis and ichthyosis vulgaris and tends to run in families with an autosomal dominant tendency
Frequently improves with age and is usually worse in winter and in dry skin
Caused by a keratin plug occluding the follicular opening, sometimes trapping a coiled hair
Usually asymptomatic and cosmetic, with a clinical diagnosis that seldom needs a biopsy
Management is symptomatic with regular emollients and keratolytics (urea, lactic acid, salicylic acid) and gentle exfoliation, and topical retinoids for resistant cases, with realistic expectations
reference.pathophysiology: Keratosis pilaris results from excessive or abnormal keratinisation of the hair-follicle infundibulum, so that a keratin plug forms and occludes the follicular opening, sometimes enclosing a coiled or trapped hair. The plug produces the palpable, rough papule, while surrounding low-grade inflammation gives the perifollicular erythema. The disorder is constitutional and often familial, and its association with atopic dermatitis and ichthyosis vulgaris reflects a shared tendency to disordered keratinisation and impaired epidermal barrier function; the atrophic facial variants involve additional follicular inflammation and scarring.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis, generally requiring no investigation
Dermoscopy showing coiled hairs and keratin plugs within follicular openings
Assessment for associated atopic dermatitis and ichthyosis vulgaris
Skin biopsy only in atypical presentations, showing follicular hyperkeratosis with a keratin plug
Consideration of an underlying syndrome when atrophy or scarring is prominent (keratosis pilaris atrophicans)
redFlags: Prominent facial erythema with scarring loss of the eyebrows suggesting a syndromic form (keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans)
Atrophy or scarring that may cause permanent hair loss
Atypical, inflammatory, or rapidly evolving lesions prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Benign and chronic but tends to improve over time, often lessening markedly by adulthood; treatment controls rather than cures, and lesions recur if therapy is stopped.
pitfalls: Over-treating a benign, cosmetic condition and causing irritation
Mistaking the atrophic facial variants for a scarring alopecia or another condition
Failing to recognise associated atopy or ichthyosis vulgaris
